slides.title: Brand Architecture & Portfolio
slides.subtitle: Every brand is a system of brands. The question is whether you designed the system or inherited it.

slides.title: P&G is invisible on purpose
slides.lead: Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest. Most shoppers have no idea these share a parent company.
bullets: They live in separate aisles, speak to separate anxieties, compete in separate categories. **That invisibility is a structural decision, not an oversight.**
Now Google: Search, Android, YouTube, Maps, Gmail, Waymo. Some carry the name prominently. Others barely mention it.
Waymo almost never leads with the Google name in consumer communications — even though it is fully owned, and even though the name would presumably carry trust.
That distance is a decision too.

slides.title: The previous chapters treated a brand as one standalone thing
slides.lead: Most real brand work does not look like that.
bullets: **Brand architecture** specifies how a company's brands relate to each other, how equity flows among them, what names appear on what offerings, and how risk is contained when something goes wrong.
Most real brand work is portfolio work: where the master brand appears, how new products get named, which connections to make visible and which to hide.
Yes — even a personal brand has sub-brands. You have offerings, and they already relate to each other whether or not you decided how.

slides.title: One axis, and everything real happens in the middle
slides.lead: Aaker and Joachimsthaler's spectrum maps the structural options between two poles. Understanding the poles first makes the middle legible.
slides.why: chapter: "maps the structural options along a spectrum between two poles" and "where the master brand and individual offerings share different degrees of connection"; fig-01 runs branded house → sub-brand → endorsed → house of brands with shared equity rising one way and risk containment the other

data.lowLabel: risk contained · every brand built from scratch

rungs.note: P&G, Unilever — the parent stays invisible

slides.title: Every launch pays into the same pool
slides.lead: One master brand, stretched across all offerings. iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch. FedEx Express, Ground, Freight, Office.
bullets: Marketing investment in one offering benefits all the others. A new product **starts with the parent's trust already in its pocket.**
The reputation you cultivate for being good at X transfers, to some degree, when you launch Y.
The cost is exposure. Shared equity is shared risk — and the damage does not stay where it started.

slides.title: One offering fails. Where does the damage land?
slides.lead: This is the whole trade-off, and you make it before you know which offering will be the one that fails.
slides.why: chapter puts the two cases side by side: "When Samsung's Note 7 batteries caught fire in 2016, the crisis hit the Samsung master brand, not just the Note line" versus "If Axe has a brand image crisis, Dove is unaffected — the two brands do not share equity in the consumer's mind, so the failure does not propagate"

tracks.label: Branded house · one shared name
notes: the crisis hit the master brand
every product was suddenly associated with it

slides.title: Surgical targeting, paid for in full
slides.lead: A portfolio of independent brands, each with its own name, identity and audience — and a parent consumers largely never encounter.
bullets: Tide for heavy-duty cleaning, Dawn for dishes, Mr. Clean for surfaces. Each speaks to a specific occasion **without diluting the others.**
The cost is economic. You cannot transfer equity from Tide to a new launch — consumers do not know the connection exists.
Every new brand needs its own advertising, its own identity work, its own distribution. P&G and Unilever can amortize that across enormous businesses. **Most organizations cannot.**

slides.title: Whose name is on it?
slides.lead: Same question, four portfolios, two completely different answers.
slides.why: chapter enumerates each parent's children by name: "iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV+, and the App Store"; "FedEx Express, FedEx Ground, FedEx Freight, FedEx Office"; "Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest, Bounty, Dawn, Febreze"; "Dove, Axe, Hellmann's, Ben & Jerry's, Lipton" — a two-level taxonomy, and P&G is named the textbook case

slides.title: Sub-brand and endorsed brand are opposite orientations
slides.lead: The poles are analytically clean and practically rare. Two intermediate structures do most of the real work.
bullets: A **sub-brand** attaches a qualifier to the master. Apple → iPhone. The master leads; the sub-brand borrows almost all its equity and exists to make the offering *nameable*, not to build independent identity.
The trade-off is dependency: **the sub-brand is only as strong as the master.**
An **endorsed brand** reverses it. Courtyard *by* Marriott. The child leads with its own identity; the parent is a trust shortcut that reduces the risk of trying something new.
Marriott runs Ritz-Carlton and St. Regis alongside Fairfield and Aloft. Putting the name prominently on all of them would blur the distinctions that make each legible.

slides.title: How much does it want to borrow, and how much does it need to differ?
slides.lead: That is the entire decision between sub-brand and endorsement.
bullets: Same audience, same category, same associations → **the sub-brand structure usually works.**
Different audience, different category, or deliberately different associations → **the endorsed or independent structure usually serves better.**
Note what is *not* on this list: which one sounds more impressive. That is not an input.

slides.title: Leverage is real. So is the thing it costs you.
slides.lead: A brand extension deploys existing equity in a new direction rather than building from scratch.
bullets: **Line extension** stays in the category: Tide Original, Free & Gentle, Pods, with Bleach. **Category extension** crosses out of it: Apple from computers to music players to phones to watches.
The launch cost of an extension is substantially lower than building a new brand. For a brand with genuine, relevant equity in the new space, that leverage is real.
The danger is dilution. Kapferer's *elastic brand*: stretch too far and the name loses the specific tension that made it useful.
Apple into groceries, insurance and furniture would stop meaning *beautifully designed technology* and start meaning *premium things, broadly*. **That diffusion is permanent.**

slides.title: Two questions, in this order
slides.lead: The chapter gives you a sequence, not a scorecard. Both questions are about the parent, not the new product.
slides.why: chapter: "The extension decision requires two questions. First: is the extension *relevant* to the parent brand's core associations? ... Second: does the extension *reinforce* or *blur* what the parent brand means?" — ordered, and no verdict is given for the reader's own case

gates.label: Relevance
gates.rule: same skills, same audience, same emotional territory — or a reach for revenue?

gates.label: Reinforce or blur
gates.rule: does the parent get more specific, or harder to locate mentally?

output.label: launch it under the parent's name

slides.title: Only one quadrant is named a danger zone
slides.lead: Fit with the parent's core associations on one axis; effect on those associations on the other.
slides.why: chapter's extension-risk figure sets "fit with the parent brand (low to high)" against "effect on parent associations (blurs to reinforces)" and flags the low-fit, blurs quadrant — Apple into groceries or insurance — as the danger zone; the other two quadrants the chapter does not adjudicate

slides.title: Co-branding and ingredient branding
slides.lead: Not all brand relationships are internal. Two independent brands can combine equity deliberately.
bullets: **Co-branding** pairs two consumer brands: Nike × Apple, Supreme × Louis Vuitton, BMW × Louis Vuitton. Each works because the pairing *reinforces* both positions — athletic performance and technology, street culture and luxury.
The co-brand is more than the sum because **the pairing itself communicates something neither brand could say alone.**
**Ingredient branding** makes a component visible inside a finished product. Intel Inside. Gore-Tex tags on outerwear.
It works when the component carries associations the manufacturer cannot independently claim — and when consumers know what the component does.

slides.title: You inherit the partner's reputation. And the partner's crises.
slides.lead: Both structures carry the risk in both directions, and you signed for it when you signed the deal.
bullets: When a partner faces a scandal or a product failure, the association you spent money building **becomes a liability.**
The financial crisis that hit various luxury brands' collaborative partners in 2008 dragged down collaborating fashion houses that had done nothing wrong.
**Choosing a co-brand partner is choosing which risks to take on board.** That is the sentence to keep.

slides.title: More brands usually means less total value
slides.lead: The intuition runs the other way — more coverage, more targeting, more options. In practice it does not.
bullets: Portfolio bloat splits marketing attention, budget and organizational energy across offerings that **cannibalize each other's audiences**.
When a company has more brands than it can actively invest in, the rest free-ride on equity that is quietly depreciating without maintenance.
The discipline is the same as segmentation: every brand must earn its place by carrying distinct associations **no other brand in the portfolio can carry.**
Redundancy is expensive even when each individual offering is good.

slides.title: The most significant portfolio moves are subtractions
slides.lead: Unilever's "Brand Imprint" programme, launched in the early 2000s. P&G made similar moves after 2014.
slides.why: chapter states the only rates in the chapter: "reduced their portfolio from approximately 1,600 brands to 400 — and revenue per brand increased"; the revenue figure itself is never given, and your own survivors are unknown

slides.title: Four offerings, one name — until one of them isn't
slides.lead: A newsletter, a course, a consulting practice, an open-source library. Same person. Not necessarily the same brand.
slides.why: chapter's worked example maps exactly this portfolio and pulls one offering out: "the library runs as an endorsed brand — 'DataPrep, from Nik Bear Brown' — or fully independently" because it "reaches a different audience... and carries different associations"; the reader's own offerings are unmapped

slides.title: Which of yours earns its place?
slides.lead: Once the map is visible, the prune candidates are usually obvious — the offerings neither building distinct equity nor making the master brand more coherent.
slides.why: chapter gives the sorting rule — "every brand must earn its place by carrying distinct, valuable associations that a different brand in the portfolio cannot carry" — and applies it to exactly one offering (the library, on different audience and different associations). It sorts nothing else, and counts nothing

data.note: The chapter maps the portfolio. It refuses to prune yours.

slides.title: A system with no architect
slides.lead: Frederick Brooks managed IBM's System/360 and its operating system in the 1960s, then wrote *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975).
bullets: His most durable idea is **conceptual integrity**: a system reflecting one coherent set of design ideas is better to use than one packed with more features built by many hands pulling in different directions.
And the integrity has to be **imposed deliberately** — it never emerges on its own.
A portfolio that accumulates through acquisitions and one-off launches is Brooks's system-without-an-architect: feature-rich, internally inconsistent, expensive to use.
Brand architecture and the pruning discipline are how you reimpose conceptual integrity on a portfolio.

slides.title: The framework is descriptive. It is not predictive.
slides.lead: I would rather you hold this loosely than hold it wrongly.
bullets: The Aaker–Joachimsthaler spectrum maps the options. It does **not** provide a strong theory of when each structure produces better outcomes — the empirical evidence is mixed and the confounds are severe.
The mechanism by which a bad extension dilutes a parent is not fully understood. The rate, the permanence, the reversibility — not well specified.
Kapferer's elastic brand is intuitive but it is **not a model**.
I do not know how to predict in advance whether a specific extension will dilute, and **I am skeptical of anyone who claims to.**

slides.title: Map every public thing you have shipped. Then name the one that is redundant.
slides.lead: Offering · relationship to the master brand · the equity it borrows · the overlap risk it creates. Four columns. Then say out loud which offering is neither building distinct equity nor making your name more coherent — and give the evidence. The map is the easy half.
